- Define ethics and apply the Golden Rule in the context of data science.
- Recognize that data comes from real people and communities, especially in minority health research.
- Identify how bias and underrepresentation affect fairness in health data analysis.
- Explain why reproducibility and transparency are ethical practices.
- Apply the Ethical Matrix framework to structure ethical decision-making.
- Discuss the balance between privacy and open data sharing.

::::::::::::::::::::::::::::::::::::::::::::::::::

:::::::::::::::::::::::::::::::::::::::: questions

- What do we mean by "ethics" in data science?  
- How does the history of minority health research shape today’s ethical responsibilities?  
- How can bias creep into data, and what are its consequences?  
- Why is reproducibility a matter of ethics, not just good practice?  
- How can we use the Ethical Matrix to evaluate difficult data decisions?  
- When should health data be shared openly, and when should it be restricted?  

::::::::::::::::::::::::::::::::::::::::::::::::::



## Foundations: What is Ethics?

Ethics provides principles for deciding right from wrong in human actions.  
It is not the same as law or compliance: something can be legal but still unethical.  

A useful framing is the **Golden Rule**: *Do unto others as you would have them do unto you.*  
This principle is powerful for thinking about how our data practices affect other people.  

:::::::::::::::::::::::::::::::::::::::::  callout


### Case Example: Tuskegee Syphilis Study

From 1932 to 1972, Black men in Alabama were misled and denied treatment in the Tuskegee Syphilis Study. The study began, perhaps, with good intentions: to study the progression of (what was at that time) and incurable disease. However, in 1940, the purified penicillin compound was isolated, and in 1943 it was used to treat syphilis for the first time (with miraculous results). By 1945 this compound was widely available to treat infections in the United States and Western Europe. This debilitating and deadly disease was no longer incurable!

However, this story does not have the happy ending we should expect. The scientists and clinicians of the United States Public Health Service, which were running the study did not treat the men in their care with the newly-available lifesaving antibiotic. Instead, these scientists:

- withheld the diagnosis of syphilis from these men, instead describing their ailments as "bad blood", making informed consent impossible
- withheld the treatment for syphilis from these men, even after treatment of syphilis with penicilin-based antibiotics was commonplace (meaning that the scientists caused harm by inaction)

> "By 1943, when the Division of Venereal Diseases began treating syphilitic patients nationwide with penicillin, the men in the Tuskegee study were not considered patients. They were viewed as experimental subjects and were denied antibiotic treatment. - *"Bad Blood:" A Case Study of the Tuskegee Syphilis Project*, <https://cales.arizona.edu/classes/pls595d/Assignments/2007/BadBlood.pdf>

This is one of the most infamous examples of failing to follow even basic ethical principles.  

- What would "do unto others" have meant in this case?  
- How would the study have looked if the Golden Rule were applied?  

::::::::::::::::::::::::::::::::::::::::::::::::::



## Data Comes From People

Every dataset reflects real people, often from communities with histories of marginalization. Participants in clinical trials often "loan" their data to researchers to complete specific research questions. For example, a patient with colon cancer may donate tissue samples to a data bank for the **purpose** of researching a cure for colon cancer. Because of this, most human subjects data comes with the restrictions that the data are to be used to better human health, most often specifically including *benefiting* the health of the person who supplied their data (this is the concept of *beneficence*: that the welfare of the participant should be the priority). Respect requires informed consent, privacy protection, and ensuring benefits from scientific discoveries flow back to individuals and communities. 

> To consider: if I were analyzing your data, are their some questions you wouldn't want me to ask?

Beyond this, we must recognize that scientific advancements are data driven. Therefore, in order to promote equitable distributions of scientific advancement, we must provide equitable opportunity for communities to provide samples. In 2000, the National Institutes of Health issued notices to all clinical trials that women and racial/ethnic minorities **must** be represented in trial cohorts (<https://grants.nih.gov/grants/guide/notice-files/NOT-OD-00-048.html>). These policies promote data collection procedures which are fair.

:::::::::::::::::::::::::::::::::::::::::  callout


### Case Examples

- **Havasupai Tribe DNA Samples (2000s):** DNA given for diabetes research was later used for other studies without consent, leading to mistrust  (<https://journalofethics.ama-assn.org/article/genetic-research-among-havasupai-cautionary-tale/2011-02>). 
- **COVID-19 Data Gaps:** Early U.S. pandemic reporting undercounted impacts on Black and Latino communities, delaying targeted responses (<https://doi.org/10.1177/00333549231154577>).  
- **All of Us Database:** The Researcher Workbench (which controls access to the *All of Us* database) requires the users to follow a code of conduct which prohibits using data for stigmatizing research (<https://www.researchallofus.org/faq/policy-on-stigmatizing-research/>).

**Challenge 1**  

Consider an academic research institution which is collecting genomic samples to complete an Alzheimer's Disease study. When people are signing the consent forms, they are given four options:

> A) My samples should be used for this study only.
  B) Request in writing for my approval to use my samples for each new study.
  C) I approve use of use my samples for other any biomedical research studies at this institution, but inform me in writing for each new study.
  D) My samples may be used for any biomedical research studies at this institution at any time and without my written permission or knowledge.

Which option would you pick? For each of the options above, describe a person who you could imagine selecting that option. What is a reason *they* would choose that option?

## Bias and Fairness in Data

If we want to mitigate biased results from our statistical models, we must cast a "wide net" to collect representative data from across the spectrum of possible patients. As we saw above, minority participants in clinical trials have not always been afforded the same protections or benefits as their majority counterparts. In some extreme examples, minority subjects were even harmed. These actions from scientists have eroded trust in medical science. Often due to this lack of trust, minority groups are often skeptical of the benefits of participating in scientific research, leading to lower participation rates among minority groups (<https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3222419/>). 

While modern clinical trials and surveillance data sets (since 2015) often have rich(er) minority representation, this was not often the case. This figure shows the average clinical trial participation for US racial/ethnic minority groups since 1990 for both NIH-funded and other-funded clinical trials^[Note that these percentages are MUCH higher for NIH-funded research alone, but their trials are smaller.]:
```{r, echo=FALSE, message=FALSE}

# Code from Claude; 7 October 2025
# Prompt: Hi Claude, I'm looking for a graph of minority representation in US
# clinical trials over time. Can you put that code into Tidyverse R code? Can
# you give me the hyperlinks of the sources you use for the data?

library(tidyverse)
library(scales)

minorityTrialParticipation_df <- tibble(
  year = c(1995, 2000, 2005, 2010, 2015, 2020),
  `African American` = c(0.97, 1.2, 1.5, 1.8, 2.0, 2.23),
  `Hispanic/Latino` = c(0.18, 0.4, 0.6, 0.8, 1.0, 1.24),
  `Asian American` = c(0.14, 0.3, 0.5, 0.7, 0.9, 1.04)
) %>%
  pivot_longer(
    cols = -year, 
    names_to = "group", 
    values_to = "percentage"
  )

### Claude Sources ###
# Based on my search results, here are the hyperlinks to the sources for the
# data:
# 
# Mayo Clinic Proceedings (2021) - Study analyzing 25 years of data showing
# African American, Hispanic/Latino, and Asian American representation trends:
# https://www.mayoclinicproceedings.org/article/S0025-6196(20)31259-3/fulltext
# 
# Lancet Regional Health - Americas (2022) - Study on racial and ethnic
# representation in clinical trials:
# https://www.thelancet.com/journals/lanam/article/PIIS2667-193X(22)00069-2/fulltext
# 
# FDA Drug Trials Snapshots - Data on demographics in clinical trials (2015-2019
# period):
# https://www.fda.gov/drugs/drug-approvals-and-databases/drug-trials-snapshots

# Create line chart for historical trends
ggplot(minorityTrialParticipation_df) +
  aes(x = year, y = percentage, color = group) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1.2) +
  geom_point(size = 3) +
  scale_color_manual(values = c(
    "African American" = "#8b5cf6",
    "Hispanic/Latino" = "#f59e0b",
    "Asian American" = "#10b981"
  )) +
  labs(
    title = "Minority Representation in US Clinical Trials Over Time",
    subtitle = "Historical trend showing modest increases in minority participation (1995-2020)",
    x = "Year",
    y = "Percentage (%)",
    color = "Minority Subgroup"
  ) +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(
    plot.title = element_text(face = "bold", size = 14),
    plot.subtitle = element_text(size = 10, color = "gray40"),
    legend.position = "bottom"
  )


```

From the perspective of statisticians, the original reason for excluding minority participants was based on good *intentions*: to reduce the extra variability and increase statistical power. However, we should not judge policies by their intentions, but by their results. The *results* of excluding minority participants from clinical trials for decades was a body of scientific research that often failed to generalize outside of the study cohort of (younger/male) white participants. The intentions might have been good, but the results were not: when minority groups are underrepresented or misclassified, then we don't get a complete picture of the disease and its effects. Skewed or incomplete data lead to biased conclusions.   

:::::::::::::::::::::::::::::::::::::::::  callout


### Case Examples

- **Pulse Oximeters:** Blood oxygen saturation readings are less accurate for patients with darker skin tones, leading to disparities in care (<https://publichealth.jhu.edu/2024/pulse-oximeters-racial-bias>).  
- **Facial Recongnition:** older facial recognition algorithms were trained primarily on white faces, so they were very inaccurate for minorities---especially for Black women (<https://amnesty.ca/features/racial-bias-in-facial-recognition-algorithms/>).
- **Electronic Health Records:** Hispanic patients are frequently misclassified as "other" or "unknown" in EHR systems, skewing analyses (<https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5342943/>).

## Reproducibility and Transparency as Ethical Practice

Reproducibility is not just a technical best practice---it is an ethical obligation.  
Transparent workflows protect against error, build trust, and make science more equitable. But before we continue our discussion, we must define terms:

> To **reproduce** scientific findings, an investigator takes the original experiment's data and sees if analysis leads to the same results. To **replicate** scientific findings, a scientist runs the same experiment and collects new data, after which analysis leads to the same [or similar] results. --- 'An Existential Crisis' for Science, 2024. <https://www.ipr.northwestern.edu/news/2024/an-existential-crisis-for-science.html>

Consider the now-famous "wolf vs. husky" image classification problem: Researchers trained a neural network to classify images as either wolves or huskies. The model achieved high accuracy on the training data, but when they investigated how it was making decisions, they discovered that the model wasn't actually learning to distinguish wolves from huskies based on the animals' *features*. Instead, it had learned that wolves tend to appear in images with snow *in the background*, while huskies were more often photographed without snow or in different settings. So the network was essentially using the presence or absence of snow as its primary classification feature, rather than actual differences between the animals (<https://dl.acm.org/doi/10.1145/2939672.2939778>).

When we perform an analysis, we should (as much as is possible), publish the original de-identified data, the source code, and directions to replicate the computing environment. When other people can see *how* we came to our conclusions, these conclusions are more trustworthy. Ethics, applied to research reproducibility, means that you make it as easy as possible for other people to reproduce your results.

:::::::::::::::::::::::::::::::::::::::::  callout


### Case Examples

- **NIH All of Us Research Program:** While this database is a large "sample of convenience", the *All of Us* program prioritizes diversity in participants and makes reproducible data pipelines available (<https://allofus.nih.gov/article/what-makes-all-us-different>).  
- **Reproducibility Crisis:** Many clinical studies fail replication, disproportionately harming underserved populations who may rely on flawed evidence. Using "open science" policies, we can reduce the potential negative impact of our own work (<https://opusproject.eu/openscience-news/he-reproducibility-crisis-how-open-science-can-save-research/>).

## Ethical Decision-Making with the Ethical Matrix

As a quick review, the Golden rule says to "do unto others as you would have done unto you." This rule has four main components in three groups:

- **do**
    1. *What* research we do?
    2. *How* we do that research?
- **others**
    3. *Who* are the people affected by your research?
- **you**
    4. *You* and your team are causing some effect to happen to others through this research

So far, we have discussed some of the many ways that the Golden Rule has been ignored in the data sciences. However, we haven't had much conversation about how we can practically apply ethical principles in data science. Given a research team and their funded research project, that team should ask questions about how the research they complete will affect various groups. The **Ethical Matrix** is a tool to help us systematically apply the Golden Rule across combinations of people and characteristics of research.

Often, two good characteristics of research may result in competing interests. For example, the value of "reproducible research" and "equity" requires that data be made publicly available to everyone, but the values of "respect for persons" and "privacy" require that data should have protected information redacted or removed. These two values are both important, but they can be in conflict. The Ethical Matrix gives research teams the structure to compare competing ethical demands upon them. This paper gives some more background and examples from the field of ecology and environmental sciences: (<https://www.frontiersin.org/journals/environmental-science/articles/10.3389/fenvs.2021.584636/full>)

We structure the sources of these competing interests in a matrix, where: 

- **Rows = stakeholders** (e.g., patients, families, community members, researchers, policymakers, taxpayers).  
- **Columns = principles** (respect for persons, well-being, autonomy, justice, beneficence, privacy, cost-effectiveness, reproducibility, accuracy, etc.).  

:::::::::::::::::::::::::::::::::::::::::  challenge

**Mini-Exercise:**  
Fill in a small Ethical Matrix for this scenario:  
*Should we release de-identified asthma data from Black and Latino children for AI research?*  

1. Who are the "others" in this case? (That is, what **rows** should your ethical matrix include?)
2. What are the characteristics of the research, the values that should be considered? (That is, what **columns** should your ethical matrix include?)
3. Use your matrix to consider:
    + Who benefits?
    + Whose autonomy is respected?
    + Who bears risks?

## Examples of Open Issues in Data Ethics
This section is not meant to be a comprehensive overview of all open ethics issues in data science, but instead to give some examples.


### Balancing Privacy and Data Sharing
Data sharing can advance science but may also compromise privacy and trust. Researchers must weigh openness (knowledge, equity) against protection (safety, respect). Two famous examples have been discussed in the past:

- **Henrietta Lacks’ HeLa Cells:** Her cells were shared without her consent. Decades after she passed away, her family was included in decisions (<https://www.smithsonianmag.com/science-nature/henrietta-lacks-immortal-cells-6421299/>).  
- **Tribal Epidemiology Centers:** American Indian and Alaskan Native tribes assert "data sovereignty" and control over their own health data and records (<https://washingtonstatestandard.com/2025/03/28/tribes-long-shut-out-from-their-own-health-data-fight-for-access-and-sovereignty/>).  

:::::::::::::::::::::::::::::::::::::::::  discussion

**Discussion:**  
When should health data be shared openly, and when should it be restricted? What criteria would you use to make that decision?  

::::::::::::::::::::::::::::::::::::::::::::::::::


### Medical Advancements vs Environmental Impacts of AI
AI is a powerful tool for scientific research. Some of the discoveries that are being made right now will increase the overall health of the human species for centuries to come. However, the computing resources of AI require enormous natural resources, such as land, electricity, carbon "credits", and water. 

- **Environmental Impact of AI:** If all data centers and the servers to support AI tools were their own country, that country would be the 11th largest consumer of electricity on the planet (<https://news.mit.edu/2025/explained-generative-ai-environmental-impact-0117>).
- **Healthcare Benefits of AI:** Embedding AI into electronic health records has the potential to transform healthcare by analyzing large datasets to improve disease diagnosis, treatment planning, and clinical decision-making (<https://bmcmededuc.biomedcentral.com/articles/10.1186/s12909-023-04698-z>).


:::::::::::::::::::::::::::::::::::::::::  discussion

**Challenge:**  
How would you quantify (in a standard currency) the positive health impact of AI compared to the negative environmental impact of AI? Discuss with your fellow students.

## Wrapping Up

:::::::::::::::::::::::::::::::::::::::: keypoints

- Ethics is distinct from law and compliance; the Golden Rule is a simple starting point.  
- Data comes from real people, and respect requires cultural and historical awareness.
- Bias in data harms minority health and can reinforce inequities.  
- Reproducibility and transparency are ethical practices that protect communities.  
- The Ethical Matrix offers a structured way to weigh impacts on stakeholders.  
- Privacy and openness must be balanced thoughtfully in health research.
